name: Research and Development

claims.claim_text: Analog IP providers can spend roughly half their engineering hours on internal test-chip development rather than customer deliverables, because staying at the leading edge depends on running silicon of their own.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would even say that I think in design effort, maybe half of our engineering hours is on internal test development, test chip development, because R&D is very important for being at the leading edge.
claims.speaker: Joren Vaes
claims.episode_title: Leading Edge Analog with Joren Vaes

claims.claim_text: Foundries support IP developers by offering discounted development area on multi-project wafers, which lets small teams get test designs fabricated without funding a full mask set.
claims.quote_verbatim: They might give us a discounted development area on multi-project wafers, is what they're called, to develop stuff.
claims.speaker: Joren Vaes
claims.episode_title: Leading Edge Analog with Joren Vaes

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor performance records announced by large research labs do not correspond to purchasable parts; exotic processes such as gallium arsenide only reach ordinary products years later, once the process has spread and cheapened.
claims.quote_verbatim: they aren't real parts that you can buy. It's more of the research kind of level
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: EE Movies, Part Rants and SPICE.

claims.claim_text: Major consumer electronics manufacturers specify recycled content and disposal hazard as design constraints, advertising products built with around 30 percent recycled plastics.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're very, they're even advertising, that all their products, are designed with, you know, 30% recycled plastics
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: A company that announces an R&D increase in dollars leaves open whether the money goes to equipment or capital expenditure; a stated headcount increase is a far more specific commitment to engineering capacity.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm so used to hearing, oh, yeah, we'll spend an extra 5 million on R&D, but they don't say what. Is it equipment, capital expenditure? But they're actually specifically mentioned headcount.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bowie and The Brown Note

claims.claim_text: Agilent moved its low-end oscilloscopes from rebadged Rigol units to in-house design and manufacture, reversing a decade-long pattern of outsourcing by large American instrument makers.
claims.quote_verbatim: the big news is that Agilent are now designing and manufacturing these low-end scopes in-house. So, everyone knows that they used to rebadge the Rigol ones, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: Custom ASICs make advanced low-cost instruments possible because the R&D funding is a one-time cost: once the chip exists, each unit costs only a few dollars to produce, which smaller competitors without that R&D capability cannot match.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because once you've put in the R&D funding to do that chip, you can churn out the chip like it's nothing, you know?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor research can be done on one-centimeter wafers grown in a laboratory, but a real manufacturing process requires four- or six-inch wafers, so scaling the substrate is a distinct step between research and production.
claims.quote_verbatim: I did my PhD on one centimeter wafers that we grew in a lab. So, no, you can do a lot of R&D on that. But to get to a real manufacturing process, you need, you know, four inch, six inch.
claims.speaker: John Edmond
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: The relationship between R&D spending and output is not monotonic: a small amount of money produces nothing because the infrastructure is missing, and beyond a point additional money stops correlating with output per dollar.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you look at it as a linear relationship, it's not monotonic, right? A little bit of money at the beginning doesn't do anything, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Younker Youtube Yarling

claims.claim_text: The finding that more money does not mean more R&D output is routinely used out of context to justify budget cuts, ignoring that marginal spending buys concrete capability such as a better oscilloscope, extra parts, or another laboratory technician.
claims.quote_verbatim: Sometimes you actually need that better scope or you need extra parts or you need another technician in your lab, you know?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Younker Youtube Yarling

claims.claim_text: The floor of the R&D spending curve is absolute: zero R&D funding yields zero R&D results, so arguments about diminishing returns apply only above some non-zero level of investment.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have zero R&D money, you will get zero R&D results
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Younker Youtube Yarling

claims.claim_text: R&D spending expressed as a percentage of revenue is a misleading comparison between companies: a firm spending 2 percent of a very large revenue can outspend competitors whose combined R&D budgets are smaller, and a low percentage may reflect development offloaded onto suppliers.
claims.quote_verbatim: Apple only spends 2% of their money on R&D and they get all this output. It's like, yeah, well, they're selling consumer products and all that stuff's offloaded, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Younker Youtube Yarling

claims.claim_text: Spending on research into new markets is partly defensive: a company that does not fund the search risks a competitor reaching the market first, and a failed program can at least be written off as a market that did not exist.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're forced to because they have to spend money researching new markets. If they don't, somebody else will and they'll beat them to it if it works.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ludibrious Luxating Layout

claims.claim_text: A commonly cited cost ratio holds that development costs at least ten times as much as research and commercialization ten times as much as development, leaving research at roughly 1 percent of the total effort of bringing a technology to market.
claims.quote_verbatim: development costs at least 10 times as much as research and commercialization costs 10 times as much as development. So, in the end, research, which we think is the most important part, is only 1% of the effort.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: A memory technology demonstrated at kilobyte densities in a research laboratory has not been shown at the megabit densities a commercial product requires, so laboratory demonstrations should be assessed against the density and volume the target market needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's one thing to do it in the research lab and you've got your 2 kilobyte memory
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: When a semiconductor company under financial pressure strips R&D, the cut tends to fall on the legacy line rather than the strategic one, so 8-bit microcontroller development is sacrificed to keep 32-bit families funded, stranding usable existing IP such as PowerPC and ColdFire.
claims.quote_verbatim: we really need to keep our 32-bit micros going. And, well, the 8-bit ones, well, you know, if we're going to cut development, we may as well cut 8-bit.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Large research organizations such as MIT Lincoln Laboratory, with roughly 3,000 staff, assign a second team of senior engineers to review the team executing a major program, producing a culture of formal and informal design reviews that can become contentious.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll have a team of really smart people working on it. And then they'll have sometimes a team of really smart people kind of looking over the shoulders of the people who are kind of working on the program.
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor suppliers will go beyond their catalogue of standard building blocks for a customer if the volume justifies it, but the engineering hours they commit are billed back to the customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: Depending on your size, they may do that. If they have to put in their R&D hours, then they're going to, of course, look at it.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Continuously chasing new markets and abandoning old ones is not the only viable strategy; a company that owns a market and keeps innovating inside that space has a defensible position.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is something to be said for the company that owns a market and sticks with it and just innovates within their space
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: Automotive manufacturers reported spending roughly 20 to 25 percent of their R&D time on the hardware and software content of the vehicle itself, a share expected to grow as sensor counts per car rise into the hundreds.
claims.quote_verbatim: he said they spend 20, 25% of their R&D time just developing the hardware and software for the car
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: Research-weighted work requires many iterations through different ideas; a concept prototyped in a day demonstrates only a limited case, and expanding it to work in every case can take on the order of twenty iterations.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're doing a lot of research, then you do have to do a lot of iteration and kind of stepping through different ideas.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: Some large manufacturers substitute prize contests for internal R&D, as with a Samsung competition paying up to $10,000 for integrating a flexible screen; entrants should read the terms to see what rights they sign over.
claims.quote_verbatim: Samsung is currently running a contest for up to $10,000 basically if you integrate a flexible screen you can get up to 10 grand for it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Troubleshooting, PCBs and LEDs - Quaintized Quich Quelling

claims.claim_text: Doctoral programs allow a student to leave with a master's degree after several years of work, so the decision to continue turns on how much the candidate values research over development-type engineering.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not a reason not to do it. It's just a matter of how much you value the research over maybe development type stuff, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Agilent's New Name, Molex's New Owner and PCB artwork - Nonsensical Naming Neolatry

claims.claim_text: High-end instruments carry the margins that fund an instrument maker's R&D, but retreating from the low and mid range costs the vendor its presence on working benches and the customers who would later buy up the range.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's big margins in there which do pay for the R&D
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent's New Name, Molex's New Owner and PCB artwork - Nonsensical Naming Neolatry

claims.claim_text: DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, is part of the United States Department of Defense and funds research and development that is primarily military-focused but sometimes broad; its predecessor ARPA created the internet.
claims.quote_verbatim: DARPA is the defense advanced research project agency. Uh, it's a part of the, uh, of the department of defense in the U S and they fund all kinds of research and development
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: Once the novel phase of a hardware product is finished, the remaining work is refinement and cost reduction, which offers neither the technical challenge nor, for an already-profitable designer, the financial motivation of the original development.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no financial motivation for selling where's the party at anymore. And the, the technical side of it isn't nearly as challenging as it was when I first did it.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Todd Bailey - Embedded Embrasure Engineering

claims.claim_text: Demanding a specific return from a research program converts it into development; genuine research cannot be held to a predicted payoff even while the team is kept on track.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you expect a specific return on research, you're no longer doing research
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: SolidCon and Traveling Tech - Joined Junk Jocularity

claims.claim_text: Capital controls calibrated for production can paralyse laboratory work, as when a production facility required a thorough written justification before a second $100 multimeter could be bought.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to do a thorough justification for why we, you know, wanted the extra $100 multimeter
claims.episode_title: SolidCon and Traveling Tech - Joined Junk Jocularity

claims.claim_text: A corporate research lab can be chartered explicitly not to feed the product pipeline, instead being asked to look three to five years ahead at how emerging social, cultural and technological movements combine, which permits output ranging from CNC-heavy mechanical installations to machine learning work.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've been asked to think three to five years out
claims.speaker: Noah Feehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Noah Feehan - Biloquistic Blinking Blush

claims.claim_text: Genuine research legitimately involves isolating a team to try many approaches and accepting that failure is part of the process, since the outcome cannot be specified in advance.
claims.quote_verbatim: Sometimes you do have to lock yourself away and just go try it a bunch and then see if anything pops out.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar Factories and HVDC Lines - Pollent Power Pushing

claims.claim_text: A development program that has run five years without a single measurement of the two functions its product must perform, such as solar output and stopping a vehicle, has not been testing at all, and the absence of results is the diagnostic.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've been working on this for five years and they don't have a single test result of the solar output or the, or trying to stop a car on this thing. I mean, like the two main things this thing must do and they haven't tested it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar Factories and HVDC Lines - Pollent Power Pushing

claims.claim_text: Assembling existing components into a difficult product is development, not fundamental research; firms such as FLIR and Seek that advance the underlying sensor technology occupy a different category from companies packaging those sensors.
claims.quote_verbatim: please don't call it innovative and, you know, and research, you know, as if they're doing some fundamental research
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Worktrips and Workspaces - Junket Jactation Jiltedness

claims.claim_text: A salaried R&D engineer at a large organization can pursue longer-term work that probably will not succeed, whereas someone self-employed or close to manufacturing is constrained to work that makes money today or protects revenue already coming in.
claims.quote_verbatim: When you're working for yourself or when you're kind of a little bit more closer to manufacturing, you're stuck in that, you know, does it make money today kind of thing?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Space Bound, Again - Xtreme Xtraplanetary Xenonosocomiophobia

claims.claim_text: Startups perform development rather than foundational research, because research is expensive, fails often, and requires reserves that a young company does not have.
claims.quote_verbatim: Startups are development. They're not research. And even at big companies with, like, tons of money, you know, it's still probably not necessarily research, right? Research is hard. It's really hard. And it fails a lot. And you need a crap load of money to do it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: Amazon's Lab126 developed the Kindle and later the Fire Phone, and the failure of the phone changed the character of what the group was permitted to work on.
claims.quote_verbatim: So Amazon has some lab, what's it called? Lab 126, right? So they're the ones who actually are. They're the ones who developed the Amazon Kindle.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: The Kindle illustrates a product that does no more than it claims: restricting it to reading books is what allows battery life measured in months, and the restraint is the design decision that keeps the product viable.
claims.quote_verbatim: The Kindle was an excellent, brilliant example of a product that didn't do more than it claimed, right? It just, it was specifically for the task.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: Engineers can steer their careers by seeking work that justifies expensive components, since the interesting problems live there, whereas shaving a MOSFET cost from thirteen cents to twelve and a half cents is a different and narrower class of challenge.
claims.quote_verbatim: I try to find work that justifies the expensive parts that I like to use
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: One method for generating electronics project ideas is to keep a wide inflow of unrelated work and repeatedly ask which pieces are close to which others and whether they can be combined; most such combinations are bad, and only occasionally does one become developable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get a lot of really, just a lot of really bad ideas. But every now and then one of them, you know, one of them works out and you can, you can develop a little bit.
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Starting from a technology and hunting for an application produces a solution looking for a problem; the more reliable direction is to find problems people already have and check whether current work solves them.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of technology is just a solution looking for a problem. And that's a terrible place to be
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Corporate funding of university research is cheap relative to internal headcount: about $150,000 a year covers roughly one full-time employee plus parts, and companies expect breakthrough ideas rather than quarterly key performance indicators in return.
claims.quote_verbatim: if a company funds, let's say, $150,000 a year to a university, all right, to a university, that's a decent amount of money. But that's one employee.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Ellis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Ellis

claims.claim_text: A genuinely new semiconductor technology typically takes ten or more years from research demonstration to being stocked in one-off quantities by distributors such as Mouser or Digi-Key.
claims.quote_verbatim: This is still pretty early days, to be honest. I mean, this is like one of those 10 plus years kind of things.
claims.episode_title: Gotta Update My Dog

claims.claim_text: Work that pushes electronics beyond straightforward component integration runs on three-to-four-year product cycles rather than the six-month cycles of consumer electronics, and depends on management patient enough to accept that the result has not been done before.
claims.quote_verbatim: it definitely was not consumer electronics, which is, you know, six month timeline type stuff. It was more like three to four year product cycle type thing
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: A hands-on hardware program that supplies all tools and parts to its students charged tuition of roughly $3,500 to $4,000 per participant, with the price set so the program did not lose money each time it ran.
claims.quote_verbatim: It ranges from 3,500 bucks to four grand to come. Um, but with that you get to buy, we buy all the tools and parts.
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Simulating a real engineering department means replacing broken parts immediately rather than treating a damaged component as the end of a student's work, and shipping replacements overnight when the schedule demands it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we treat all of the students like they work in an engineering department. So if they break apart or whatever, it's not like, well, that was your part time to go home.
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Established industries outside technology often carry expensive operational problems and substantial revenue while having no internal R&D department, so they look to outside technology companies to supply innovation.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have really, really expensive problems and serious amounts of revenue. And they are trying to innovate and they don't have internal R and D departments.
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: A hardware-focused venture fund may place about a third of its capital in consumer, and deliberately co-invest with social media, industrial design or branding investors to cover the skills it lacks, in contrast to funds chasing a single outsized win to offset a hundred failures.
claims.quote_verbatim: the third of it is in consumer. And, and what we generally do when we're investing in consumers, we know what we know and we don't know what we don't know.
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: R&D grant funding restricts how recipient time is used, prohibiting salaried hours from being charged to sales and marketing work.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's an R and D grant, you know, you can't spend the money, AKA you can't spend your salary time on sales and marketing
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Ethernet was invented at Xerox PARC, but the technology was commercialized only after members of that team left to found 3Com, illustrating how research value can leave the funding organization.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Ethernet was invented there. But, you know, then the people from that team left and formed 3Com and, you know, commercialized the Ethernet there.
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: The Xerox Alto was built as a ten-year lookahead rather than a product, at an effective cost of roughly $100,000 per machine, and the approach was vindicated when the Macintosh appeared in 1984, about eleven years later, closely matching what the team had projected.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Alto was way too expensive to be sold as a product. You know, it probably was the equivalent of, you know, $100,000 per machine.
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: No present-day equivalent of Xerox PARC or Bell Labs exists as a single broad-front research institution; long-horizon work is instead split across many small groups working on specific areas such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, partly because modern problems span more disciplines.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are no Xerox parks these days. There are no Bell Labs these days. Not in terms of overall general stuff. There's lots of little groups working on specific things.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: Much consumer hardware is not R&D-centric but a repackaging of silicon vendors' reference designs, with the vendor absorbing the development cost; many consumer routers are the networking chip's reference circuit rebuilt.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just repackaging stuff that they're getting from another vendor. And it's really the vendors that are absorbing all that R&D cost for you.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Vendor example software is written for ease of evaluation and carries explicit warnings against production use with security features disabled, so shipping copied example code, such as a bundled web server, is a recognized source of insecure devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you look at the example code, it has all these warnings that say, this is – do not use in production. This does not have security kind of enabled because it makes it more complicated.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Companies rarely staff engineers to invent new products; most engineering employment is development work aimed at producing an answer and getting a design out the door, and industrial customers often outsource even that to consultancies from rough sketches.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reality is that a company is not going to hire enough engineers to have someone sitting around and dreaming up the next big thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Davis

claims.claim_text: Ladder logic persists in industrial control for a workforce reason rather than a technical one: it lets a technician with about three weeks of training program a multimillion-dollar machine, and that interchangeability of personnel also explains vendor concentration around Allen-Bradley.
claims.quote_verbatim: so that the guy who went to like three weeks of technical training can program the multimillion dollar machine. And you can pick that guy from any technical school in the U S and that's also a reason everybody uses Alan Bradley too.
claims.speaker: John Davis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Davis

claims.claim_text: A product requiring little development effort can still succeed rapidly through creative marketing, making the marketing capability rather than the technology the competitive advantage.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can take something that's relatively easy to develop. So there's not much R and D and make it explosive like overnight with a creative marketing
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: In a downturn, large companies cut research and development budgets first, and the cancellations propagate immediately to the 20- to 30-person design and development consultancies that serve them, which is how a functioning service business can collapse within months.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the first things that, uh, big companies do, which was most of their clients is they cut their research and development budgets. And that means all the small, uh, service businesses that are supporting them typically have major project cancellations
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Open exploratory hardware projects, such as successive experiments with PCB coil propulsion, function as research whose payoff depends on someone later finding an application for the technique.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is like research and development. And it's waiting for, you know, the person who has the killer app to come and find it or someone to stumble upon it
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Very low part cost generates experimentation independently of product polish: modules such as Espressif's and LoRaWAN hardware are not especially refined, but the near-absence of a price barrier puts them in far more hands.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have a wide range of people who are accessible to it. They can actually purchase it. There's almost no barrier because it is so low cost.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: A consultant should enter a fixed-bid contract only when both a deliverables list and acceptance criteria exist, meaning the specific tests and outcomes that define completion; with both in hand, estimates can land within 5 to 10 percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: I won't enter a fixed bid unless we have not only a set of deliverables, so like, these are the things I'm going to do for you but also acceptance criteria
claims.episode_title: Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: Projects that are genuinely new work from scratch cannot be priced as a fixed bid, because the work sits closer to science than engineering and its endpoint is unknown when the contract is signed.
claims.quote_verbatim: Yeah, like research-based stuff. Research-based stuff. Yeah. You can't do that fixed bid.
claims.episode_title: Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: When requirements and acceptance criteria do not yet exist, an hourly agreement with a check-in every ten hours lets the client approve or stop the work in bounded increments while the consultant buys the exploratory time needed to write a specification, after which the engagement can convert to fixed bid.
claims.quote_verbatim: Let's do an hourly agreement for now. And let's have, every 10 hours, we'll check in.
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: A consulting practice structured this way can settle at roughly three quarters fixed-bid work and one quarter hourly.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd say probably maybe half of my work, maybe three quarters is fixed bid. And then the other half or 25% is hourly.
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: Patents function as the return on R&D expenditure: a company that spends several million dollars on engineers and prototypes ends with a saleable and defensible asset it can license, sell, or use to protect the revenue that justifies the investment.
claims.quote_verbatim: patents are, are usually the thing that are, it's a return on the R and D dollars that someone spends
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Long

claims.claim_text: In legal terminology a non-practicing entity is a party that buys patents with no intention of using them; because patent litigation is very expensive to defend, nuisance suits can extract settlements smaller than the cost of fighting them.
claims.quote_verbatim: what we call a non-practicing entity where someone just buys up patents, never intending to use them
claims.speaker: Joe Long
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Long

claims.claim_text: A certified medical device whose release cycle requires three months of qualification per change makes iterative code exploration ruinously expensive, since even a one-line change carries the full three-month cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: Every time they do a release of this device, which is quite large, it takes three months to get it through the qualification process. So you make a one line change to the code and you want to do a release. It's a three month cycle.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Substituting exploration for design, having a domain expert write and play with code until behaviour seems right and then freezing it, is research being run inside a development program; in a regulated medical device it produced unending defects, FDA investigation and millions of dollars in cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: we don't really understand the mechanical interaction with things. We have to have a domain expert actually writing code and playing with it to figure out what's supposed to happen. And then once it seems to work right, then we lock down the code.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: EDA tool vendors run on small teams with limited engineering bandwidth, so effort concentrates on the core tool and component data becomes a secondary concern, leaving room for specialist suppliers of footprints and symbols.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know the challenges that EDA tools have, you know, uh, in terms of R and D and bandwidth and things like that. And, uh, yeah, they're all small, small teams to start with.
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Licensing third-party IP is low-risk where the block is not the basis of differentiation, such as video compression in a specialized product whose advantage lies elsewhere; writing the same functionality from scratch is a deliberate R&D cost taken against a long-term payoff.
claims.quote_verbatim: buying someone else's IP is not a big deal because you don't need to differentiate based on that IP
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: The point in a product line at which a team should absorb the cost of replacing bought-in IP with its own implementation is around the second or third revision, once the product has proven itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would say for me, it would be rev two or three
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: Consulting on genuinely unsolved problems means taking a client's money for work that may not succeed, which is the practical boundary between research and development in contract engineering; the clients who want those questions answered are nonetheless the most rewarding.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're taking someone's money for something that's not necessarily going to work out research versus development
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Creative Engineering with Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: Breaking a project into sub-assemblies and finishing each one individually before integration protects progress against interruptions, since a project worked on outside full-time hours will be interrupted and a half-finished whole is easier to abandon than a finished sub-assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: I like to break it down into like sort of sub assemblies, finish those individually and then start putting them together
claims.speaker: Zack Freedman
claims.episode_title: Finishing Prototypes with Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: Releasing a project so that others can build it is a separate project in its own right, requiring instructions, documentation, comment handling and ongoing support, and it should be scoped as such rather than treated as the tail end of the build.
claims.quote_verbatim: if we release the project, right? So other people can make it, that's a project in and of itself because it needs instructions, documentation, comments, support
claims.episode_title: Finishing Prototypes with Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: Component shortages suppress exploratory work directly: when lead times force immediate purchasing decisions, there is no time to do the R&D and then build a prototype, so planned investigations are skipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's stuff that we're going to do with R and D that I didn't bother. Cause it's like, I don't have time to do the R and D and then do a prototype. And like, I just need to buy stuff now.
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Under supply constraints small hardware companies must buy a hundred or two hundred parts, potentially a year's supply, for designs they are only fairly confident about and whose production may be far off, which strains businesses that normally fund each production run from the proceeds of the last.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to buy a hundred or 200, at least quantity parts for some of the stuff that I'm pretty sure we're going to end up using in the final production, but that production won't happen
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Very small companies and startups impose almost no procedural overhead on development work, which is the principal structural contrast with large defense contractors.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you work in a very small company or a startup, there's almost no red tape and R&D can be as fun as you want.
claims.speaker: Leigh Brady
claims.episode_title: Siloed Engineering with Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: A media channel can serve as the development arm of a product business, with public build videos acting as the R&D function that feeds the manufacturing and retail side.
claims.quote_verbatim: using my YouTube channel as a as an R&D department
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz
claims.episode_title: Product Design with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: Hermetic tantalum polymer capacitors are built by welding tantalum polymer pellets into a ceramic package processed like a standard hybrid microcircuit and sealing it with a non-moisture-bearing internal atmosphere.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of microcircuits, we'll have the tantalum pellets, tantalum polymer pellets. We've welded them into the material system, you know, into that ceramic package.
claims.speaker: Ron Demcko
claims.episode_title: Capacitor Schoopage with Ron Demcko from AVX

claims.claim_text: Capacitor development around forty years ago could be run on the production line itself, with single-layer parts made by taking MLCC scrap from the edges of wafer starts, grinding it down by hand, and metallizing it; that improvisation is no longer possible on modern lines.
claims.quote_verbatim: we came up with some types of single air caps by getting MLCC scrap from the sides of the wafer starts, grinding it down by hand, and then metallizing it
claims.speaker: Ron Demcko
claims.episode_title: Capacitor Schoopage with Ron Demcko from AVX

claims.claim_text: A large passive component manufacturer separates its research function into central R&D at a single site, in AVX's case Greenville, South Carolina, plus applied R&D and process R&D distributed across its worldwide plants.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've got central R&D for AVX at any rate is in Greenville, South Carolina. Then there's applied R&D and process R&D around the world.
claims.speaker: Ron Demcko
claims.episode_title: Capacitor Schoopage with Ron Demcko from AVX

claims.claim_text: At a synthetic biology startup of roughly two dozen people, a single engineer wrote the software for the hardware and also spun the PCBAs for factory instruments, illustrating how thin staffing at small companies produces unusually broad individual scope.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I think it was like employee number 24. And I was kind of the, the, the human who would write software for hardware and occasionally spin, uh, PCBAs for the instruments that were going into the factory.
claims.episode_title: Grad School Time Capsule with Joshua and Zach

claims.claim_text: Incumbent design tools are difficult to displace because each year's spending of hundreds of millions on development compounds on roughly twenty years of accumulated prior IP, alongside vendor relationships that feed the incumbent directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: each year they would put hundreds of millions of R and D into it on top of building on prior IP
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams
